outcome: No case of the problem was settled and no bound moved between 26 January 2024 and today; the only activity in the window is a continuing, high-volume stream of amateur and semi-professional claimed proofs of P=NP or P≠NP, all unverified and, per expert commentary, uniformly flawed in the recognizable ways prior claimed proofs have been flawed.

ai.basis_quote: Run your paper through an AI system, preferably a reasoning model, using the prompt 'Give me a critical review of this paper.' ... if you can't convince it, you're not going to convince me.

summary: The P versus NP problem remains formally open. Its own Wikipedia article, checked directly, states plainly that it 'remains open despite a million-dollar prize and a huge amount of dedicated research' and contains no mention of any AI-related development. Independent searches (arXiv, Google, and Lance Fortnow's Computational Complexity blog, an authoritative expert digestion source for this specific problem) turn up a large and apparently growing volume of claimed proofs across 2024-2026 -- e.g. a March 2025 'A proof of P≠NP' on the Cryptology ePrint Archive, a March 2025 claim by Frank Vega that 'leading AI systems have confirmed the validity' of his P=NP proof, an April 2026 preprint by Kaoru Aguilera Katayama claiming P=NP via a 4-D Game-of-Life construction, and numerous Medium/Towards AI posts announcing AI has 'solved' or 'confirmed' P vs NP. None of these have been digested, verified, or endorsed by the complexity-theory community. Fortnow's April 2025 post ('P v NP Papers Galore') reports receiving roughly seven such claims in two weeks (well above his usual rate of one per month), places them into the same recurring categories of error seen for decades (unjustified assumptions about machine behavior, algorithms that only work on small test cases, philosophical reframing rather than mathematical argument), and states such papers 'rarely (really never) provide new insights.' Notably, Fortnow's own suggested use of AI is exactly the kind of role that does NOT count under this scheme: he recommends authors ask a reasoning model to critique their own paper before sending it to him -- i.e., AI as a proofreading/sanity-check gate, not as a producer of mathematical content. The claims that do invoke AI (Vega's 'AI confirmed my proof', ChatGPT-4 'reviewing' a 12-paper submission and finding no flags) describe AI checking or endorsing human-authored arguments, not AI producing an argument, construction, or case that entered any accepted result -- and none of the underlying proofs is itself accepted, so there is no settled mathematical content for AI to have contributed to in the first place. This is a clean 'nothing happened' case under the scope rule in section 3: no case of the stated problem was settled, no bound on any open sub-question moved, and the recurring claims are uniformly rejected variants/errors rather than admitted partial results.
competing_reading: One could argue the sheer volume and persistence of AI-'endorsed' claims (Vega's repeated ResearchGate posts, the 12-paper Coq-core submission reviewed favorably by ChatGPT-4, the Medium/Towards AI pieces explicitly titled 'AI Solves The P Versus NP Problem') constitutes an 'incident' worth recording as progress/ai_role=incident, since these are AI-adjacent claims that were at least implicitly withdrawn by community non-acceptance. I did not code it this way because none of these claims was ever accepted, published, or treated as live by any expert -- there was no rise-then-fall trajectory of acceptance to withdraw, just perpetual, ambient rejection, which is qualitatively different from the 'announced claim later retracted' pattern the incident code is meant to capture. If a future record-keeper judges that the volume itself is the notable event, `progress`/`incident` dated to, e.g., the April 2025 Vega claim would be the alternative classification.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an expert digestion (Fortnow, Aaronson, or a journal of record) stating that any specific 2024-2026 claimed proof withstood scrutiny -- none currently exists -- or (b) an authors' account, for any accepted or even seriously-considered partial result, stating that an AI system produced part of the mathematical argument rather than merely checking or critiquing human-produced work.
